final_proof:
**Claim.** For every prime $p$, the set $\mathbb{Q}_p$ of $p$-adic numbers is uncountable.

**Setup and conventions.** For a nonzero rational $x$, write $x = p^{v}\,\frac{r}{s}$ with $v\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $r,s$ integers not divisible by $p$; the integer $v = v_p(x)$ is uniquely determined, and $|x|_p = p^{-v_p(x)}$, $|0|_p = 0$. This is the $p$-adic absolute value on $\mathbb{Q}$; it is non-archimedean: $|x+y|_p \le \max(|x|_p,|y|_p)$. In particular, if $x = p^m N$ with $N\in\mathbb{Z}$, then $|x|_p \le p^{-m}$ (since $v_p(N)\ge 0$ when $N\neq 0$).

$\mathbb{Q}_p$ is the completion of $(\mathbb{Q},|\cdot|_p)$: a field containing (an isometric copy of) $\mathbb{Q}$, with an absolute value $|\cdot|_p$ extending that of $\mathbb{Q}$, which is complete with respect to the metric $d(x,y)=|x-y|_p$. (Concretely, $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is the set of equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences in $(\mathbb{Q},|\cdot|_p)$, two sequences being equivalent iff their difference tends to $0$; everything below applies verbatim to that construction.) We use only: (i) $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq\mathbb{Q}_p$ with $|\cdot|_p$ extended; (ii) completeness; (iii) the reverse triangle inequality $\big||x|_p-|y|_p\big|\le |x-y|_p$, valid for any absolute value, which makes $|\cdot|_p$ continuous.

Let $S = \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of all sequences $a=(a_0,a_1,a_2,\dots)$ with each $a_i\in\{0,1\}$. Note $0,1 < p$ since $p\ge 2$.

**Step 1: $S$ is uncountable.** Suppose $f:\mathbb{N}\to S$ is any map; write $f(n) = (f(n)_0, f(n)_1,\dots)$. Define $c\in S$ by $c_n = 1 - f(n)_n$. For each $n$, $c_n \ne f(n)_n$, so $c\neq f(n)$. Hence no map $\mathbb{N}\to S$ is surjective. Since $S$ is also infinite (e.g. the sequences with a single $1$ in position $j$, $j\in\mathbb{N}$, are pairwise distinct), $S$ is neither finite nor countably infinite, i.e. $S$ is uncountable.

**Step 2: a map $\Phi : S\to\mathbb{Q}_p$.** For $a\in S$ and $n\ge 0$, put
$$s_n(a) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i p^i \in \mathbb{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{Q}.$$
For $n>m$, $s_n(a)-s_m(a) = \sum_{i=m}^{n-1} a_i p^i = p^m \sum_{i=m}^{n-1} a_i p^{i-m}$, which is $p^m$ times an integer, so $|s_n(a)-s_m(a)|_p \le p^{-m}$. Given $\varepsilon>0$ choose $M$ with $p^{-M}<\varepsilon$; then for all $n>m\ge M$, $|s_n(a)-s_m(a)|_p\le p^{-m}\le p^{-M}<\varepsilon$. Thus $(s_n(a))_n$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb{Q}$, hence in $\mathbb{Q}_p$, and by completeness it converges to a unique element $\Phi(a)\in\mathbb{Q}_p$. (In the Cauchy-sequence model, $\Phi(a)$ is simply the class of $(s_n(a))_n$.)

**Step 3: $\Phi$ is injective.** Let $a,b\in S$ with $a\ne b$. The set $\{i\in\mathbb{N}: a_i\ne b_i\}$ is nonempty, so it has a least element $k$. Then $a_i=b_i$ for $i<k$ and $a_k-b_k = \pm 1$. For every $n>k$,
$$s_n(a)-s_n(b) = \sum_{i=k}^{n-1}(a_i-b_i)p^i = p^k\Big((a_k-b_k) + p\,N_n\Big),\qquad N_n=\sum_{i=k+1}^{n-1}(a_i-b_i)p^{i-k-1}\in\mathbb{Z}.$$
The integer $(a_k-b_k)+pN_n = \pm1 + pN_n$ is congruent to $\pm 1 \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$, so it is nonzero and not divisible by $p$. Hence $v_p(s_n(a)-s_n(b)) = k$ exactly, i.e.
$$|s_n(a)-s_n(b)|_p = p^{-k}\quad\text{for all } n>k.$$
Now $s_n(a)-s_n(b)\to \Phi(a)-\Phi(b)$ in $\mathbb{Q}_p$ (since $|(s_n(a)-s_n(b)) - (\Phi(a)-\Phi(b))|_p \le |s_n(a)-\Phi(a)|_p + |s_n(b)-\Phi(b)|_p\to 0$), and by the reverse triangle inequality
$$\big|\,|s_n(a)-s_n(b)|_p - |\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)|_p\,\big| \le |(s_n(a)-s_n(b))-(\Phi(a)-\Phi(b))|_p \to 0.$$
Therefore $|\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)|_p = \lim_{n}|s_n(a)-s_n(b)|_p = p^{-k} > 0$, so $\Phi(a)\neq\Phi(b)$. (In the Cauchy-sequence model this says exactly that $(s_n(a)-s_n(b))_n$ does not tend to $0$, so the two sequences are inequivalent.)

**Step 4: conclusion.** Suppose, for contradiction, that $\mathbb{Q}_p$ were countable. Then its subset $\Phi(S)$ is countable (a subset of a countable set is countable). Since $\Phi$ is injective (Step 3), $\Phi : S\to\Phi(S)$ is a bijection, so $S$ would be countable, contradicting Step 1. Hence $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is uncountable. $\blacksquare$

*Remark.* If one instead defines $\mathbb{Q}_p$ via $p$-adic expansions $\sum_{i\ge m} d_i p^i$ with digits $d_i\in\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ (distinct digit sequences giving distinct $p$-adic numbers), the map $a\mapsto\sum_{i\ge0}a_ip^i$ is injective on $S$ immediately, and Steps 1 and 4 give the same conclusion; Steps 2–3 show this identification is consistent with the completion definition.
